sections.gloss: Post-phenomenology (Ihde) as critique + continuation; five differences from classical phenomenology; humans and technologies as interrelational and mutually co-constitutive
Ihde's four mediation relations (embodiment, hermeneutic, background, alterity) replacing the bare present-at-hand / ready-to-hand pair; cites Technics and Praxis (1979)
Mediation as constitutive (Verbeek mediators-not-intermediaries; Latour); Airbnb and gun examples; context = 'with text'; three points of mediation
Latour actant/script/delegation; Wimsatt-Beardsley intentional fallacy -> Ihde designer fallacy; Husserl intentionality; Franssen for-ness; creative misuse
Ihde's central concept: technology 'is what it does / what it can be'; schizofunctionality (Baudrillard); Krippendorff PC; Flusser/Ingold trickster; design metaphysics
Object studies proper: Boradkar history of things; Heidegger thing/gathering/jug-void; Latour matters-of-concern; Bill Brown thing theory; Folkmann material+immaterial

key_terms.gloss: Ihde's stance: critique of classical phenomenology's technology account + continuation of Heidegger redirected to everyday/newer technologies; treats individual devices as unique
Ihde: humans and technologies are not in a one-way control relation; 'I use the pen, but the pen uses me as well'

the constitutive force that shapes the mutual relation in which subject and object are both concretely constituted; mediators 'help to constitute what is real for us', not intermediaries that merely convey
Verbeek: technologies co-shape the human world and human relations with technology; humans are 'not sovereign' but 'inextricably interwoven' with technology
Verbeek: an artifact without people relating to it is 'a piece of junk'; a technology is always a 'technology-to...', and that 'to-...' gives the artifact its identity
Latour/ANT: anything, living or non-living, that imposes intention within a system; replaces 'agent' to leave room for non-human actants
Latour: an artifact's inscribed purpose ('its affordance, its potential to take hold of passersby'); designers build prescriptions for use into the product's materiality
Latour (via Verbeek): designers delegate specific responsibilities to artifacts; to a speed bump 'the responsibility was delegated to make sure nobody drives too fast'

Ihde's coinage (parallel to the intentional fallacy): the 'deistic' notion of a designer-god whose artifact 'seems intelligent by design'; the real design process is a complex web of inter-relations among designer, materials, and uses
Wimsatt & Beardsley: judging a text by assumed authorial intent is a mistake; the text stands on its own; Ihde's template for the designer fallacy
consciousness is always consciousness OF something; makes visible the inextricable human-world connection (humans always think/see/feel something)

Franssen: technical artifacts are created with a purpose that 'clings to the artifact' after the maker leaves; natural objects are 'for something' only ephemerally; a designed object is for something as consciousness is of something

Ihde's central concept: technology has multiple stabilities in its relation to humans; it 'is what it does', takes shape by 'what it can do' not 'what it is'; scripts assert some but context-varying influence; not 'unstable'

Baudrillard: each object has a split functionality enabling it to transcend its main function and serve many purposes within a system of signs; functionality = ability to become integrated into an overall scheme
Wendt's framing: the fundamental question of what a design solution IS, what it SHOULD be, and what it CAN be; the 'can be' is a phenomenological question crucial to experience design

users breaking intended use cases (hammer-as-paperweight, screwdriver-as-lever, tie-on-doorknob); enabled by multistability; entails a shift in the object's 'mental model'; reveals un-discovered needs/wants/desires
'with text'; the peripheral information used to interpret a situation; context shapes experience and forces designers to think at the level of systems

Heidegger: 'the jug is a thing insofar as it things'; 'thing' means gathering — the bringing-together of disparate meaning (function, cultural/familial meaning, destructive power); 'thinging is the nearing of the world'
Heidegger: 'the emptiness, the void, is what does the vessel's holding'; the unseen/immaterial aspects of a thing give shape to what is designed
Bill Brown: 'we look through objects but only catch a glimpse of things'; we confront the thingness of objects when they stop working for us (the drill breaks, the car stalls)
Latour: as matters of fact become matters of concern, objects are turned into things 'rendered into objects of design through and through'
the cluster of movements (post-phenomenology, OOO, actor-network theory, thing theory) recentering objects as a primary focus for design theory

claims.text: Post-phenomenology is both a critique and a continuation of classical phenomenology: a critique of its treatment of technology, a continuation that builds on Heidegger and applies to newer/everyday technologies.

Humans and technologies are interrelational and mutually co-constitutive; neither pure humans-over-nature (Promethean) nor autonomous-technology (Frankenstein) is correct — even with a pen, the pen with its material selectivities 'uses' me as well.
Ihde's four interaction styles assume each device is unique in how it participates in generating meaning, avoiding the assumption that objects are simply neutral tools humans use to accomplish goals.

Background relations are shaped by lack of conscious awareness (Verbeek), but Wendt qualifies this as 'unnecessarily restrictive': experience is shaped by both conscious and non-conscious factors; the embodied/background difference is one of proximity and direct involvement, not awareness.

Heidegger took technology as the way worldly meaning was disclosed to Dasein, whereas Ihde concentrated on interactions with individual devices as the starting point; each device interaction produces a unique disclosure, opening the possibility to design for particular meanings rather than a generic revealing of essence.

Objects obtain identity through human interaction just as users gain self-understanding through objects: a desk is only a desk in relation to what we do with it; 'desk-ness' is nothing in the word but only what we do with the desk.
Objects are not neutral aspects of the environment but active participants in human-environment systems; recognizing their active role is a crucial, ethical responsibility for designers.

There is a reciprocal relationship between social relations and objects: relations result in objects, which result in new relations; technology must be analyzed for the role it plays in social processes, not only the processes that construct it.

Mediating technologies are mediators, not intermediaries: they do not merely convey the objective world to subjects' minds but help to constitute what is real for us and what we are in relation to that reality.

Mediation is a constitutive act, not a simple interplay between subject and object; the gun and its user combine into a 'gunman', a new hybrid entity different from either alone — the gun mediates the situation to create reality.

Three points: (1) technology mediates the relationship between self and world; (2) mediation helps constitute the entire experience, not merely intervene between poles; (3) movement between interaction styles can be quite fluid.
Function plus situated meaning ('here and now') are the fuel of mediation; no other artifact can be this specific material thing, here and now.

Designers create the conditions of possibility for desired outcomes but cannot guarantee them; strong, clearly articulated intent is necessary to balance mediation, but one must know the limits of intentionality and avoid the linear problem-to-solution trap.
A tool is 'the extension of social skills to nonhumans' (Latour); this is best read as recognition that objects can change systems and can mediate, speak, and manipulate as human actants do.

Delegation can offload moral responsibility onto objects (speed bump, weighted hotel key, automatic seat belt); the UX mantra 'don't make me think' can become jarring when it strips agency from the human actant.

The designer fallacy (Ihde) is 'deistic': it imagines a designer-god whose artifact seems intelligent by design; in fact the design process is a far more complex set of inter-relations among designer, materials, and uses, offering a multitude of alternate uses beyond original intention.

Design outcomes are emergent: 'a genuine conversation is never the one that we wanted to conduct' (Gadamer); the designer creates conditions of possibility, but actual outcomes lie outside both designer and user, in a system of designers, users, and object/experience.

A designed object is FOR something as consciousness is OF something (Husserl/Franssen); technical artifacts carry scripts that 'cling to the object' after the maker leaves, while natural objects' physical properties communicate potential use (foreshadowing affordances).

Multistability holds that technology takes shape not according to what it is but according to what it can do; an instrument 'is what it does, and this in a context of assignments' (Ihde) — no technology is one thing or incapable of belonging to multiple contexts.

A technology's mediating capacity is no essential property of things themselves but emerges from the interplay of things and context: technologies 'are what they are only within the context in which they are used'.

The fundamental question of design metaphysics is what a design solution is, should be, and can be; concern with what the solution CAN be is as fundamental to design as the future-facing nature of abductive thinking.
Every object of design 'sets a trap by presenting a problem in the form of what appears to be its solution' (Ingold); the designer is a trickster whose field is the management of imperfection.

Creative misuse involves a metaphysical shift: not only is the object used otherwise, its cognitive designation / 'mental model' changes (a screwdriver used not as 'screwdriver' but as 'lever'); the identity of the object depends on how it is used.

The roles of designer, maker, and user are distinguishable but not rigorously distinct; if things are never finished, design can no longer be sharply distinguished from making (Ingold), so thinking in systems becomes paramount.

Experience is always OF something, so designing an experience depends on designing the objects of experience; but experience design is really concerned not with objects as such but with the effects objects have on intangible systems of meaning.

The thing 'things' (Heidegger): it gathers and presents meaning; the unseen aspects — the emptiness, the void of the jug — are what give shape to what is designed, so experience design must attend to the interaction of tangible and intangible.

Heidegger forgets two points: (1) designers CAN design at a systems level, influencing how the thing things; (2) the object does not merely exist apart from the maker but 'things on its own' with multistable tendencies across contexts — where experience designers play.

interlocutors.name: Don Ihde
interlocutors.work: Technics and Praxis (1979); later work incl. designer-fallacy essay
interlocutors.draws: the chapter's spine: post-phenomenology; the four mediation relations; the designer fallacy; multistability ('an instrument is what it does'; 'what it can do'). Adopted as the engine of Wendt's design theory.

interlocutors.name: Peter-Paul Verbeek
interlocutors.draws: embodied<->hermeneutic continuum; precise background-relation definition; co-shaping/'not sovereign' account of mediation; 'technology-to...'; the Ihde-vs-Heidegger disclosure contrast. Wendt's main conduit for Ihde/Latour, but he QUALIFIES Verbeek's conscious-awareness-only view of background relations.

interlocutors.name: Bruno Latour
interlocutors.work: actor-network theory ('What is a tool?'; We Have Never Been Modern; the speed-bump/key/seat-belt studies)
interlocutors.draws: actant; script/affordance; delegation; matters-of-fact -> matters-of-concern. Non-human-agency framework; Wendt flags Latour's loose use of 'affordance'.

interlocutors.name: Graham Harman (OOO)
interlocutors.draws: named (with ANT and thing theory) as a movement recentering objects as a primary focus for design ('object studies'); aligned with the chapter's turn without working its metaphysics in detail.

interlocutors.name: Edmund Husserl
interlocutors.draws: consciousness is always consciousness OF something; grounds the inextricable human-world link that post-phenomenology radicalizes.

interlocutors.name: Martin Heidegger
interlocutors.work: Being and Time (equipment); 'The Thing'; The Question Concerning Technology; What Is Called Thinking?
interlocutors.draws: the critiqued-yet-continued source: ready-to-hand, standing-reserve, and the late 'thing that things'/gathering/jug; 'language remains the master of man'. Wendt builds on and CORRECTS him (systems-level design; the object's own multistable thinging).

interlocutors.name: Maarten Franssen
interlocutors.draws: the 'for-ness' of technical artifacts vs. the ephemeral purpose of natural objects; blurs the natural/artificial distinction in use.

interlocutors.name: Donald Schon
interlocutors.draws: design as a 'reflective conversation with the situation' in which the situation 'talks back'.

interlocutors.name: Hans-Georg Gadamer
interlocutors.draws: 'a genuine conversation is never the one that we wanted to conduct'; deepens Schon into emergent, non-willed design outcome.

interlocutors.name: Wimsatt & Beardsley
interlocutors.draws: judging a text by assumed authorial intent is a mistake; the text stands on its own; Ihde's template for the designer fallacy.

interlocutors.name: Jean Baudrillard
interlocutors.draws: functionality as integration into an overall scheme; the system of objects is schizofunctional (each object split to serve many purposes).

interlocutors.name: Klaus Krippendorff
interlocutors.draws: multistability as generative — the PC born by combining the typewriter and TV screen as metaphors.

interlocutors.name: Vilem Flusser
interlocutors.draws: 'design' rooted in deceit/trickery; the machine that cheats nature (the lever cheats gravity).

interlocutors.name: Tim Ingold
interlocutors.draws: the designer as trickster; 'every object of design sets a trap'; 'can design any longer be distinguished from making?'

interlocutors.name: Prasad Boradkar
interlocutors.draws: the capsule history of philosophies of things (Thales -> Heidegger -> Latour), framing the phenomenology->post-phenomenology progression.

interlocutors.name: Bill Brown
interlocutors.draws: 'we look through objects but only catch a glimpse of things'; thingness surfaces in breakdown.

interlocutors.name: Mads Folkmann
interlocutors.work: The Aesthetics of Imagination in Design
interlocutors.draws: both material and immaterial effects are at work when design enters the human domain of evoking meaning.

interlocutors.name: Lucy Kimbell
interlocutors.draws: objects are of immense importance to design discourse and are often the end result of a design process.

interlocutors.name: Maurice Merleau-Ponty
interlocutors.draws: the body-thing-world unity; the body is known precisely only as it moves toward a thing.

interlocutors.name: Samuel Beckett
interlocutors.draws: literary illustration of objects giving life meaning and gaining identity through use.

design_principles.name: Design for particular meanings, not generic essence
design_principles.gloss: Because each device discloses uniquely, target specific meanings rather than a generic revealing of essence.

design_principles.name: Design for the object acting back (mediation)
design_principles.gloss: Treat objects as active participants; account for how the object acts back upon the user; recognizing this active role is a crucial ethical responsibility.

design_principles.name: Design at the level of systems / context
design_principles.gloss: Context and mediation force systems-level thinking; research and foresight must probe the periphery and the web of relations, not the isolated object.

design_principles.name: Hold strong-but-bounded intent
design_principles.gloss: Articulate clear intent to balance mediation, while knowing its limits and avoiding the problem-to-solution trap and the designer fallacy.

design_principles.name: Delegate responsibly
design_principles.gloss: Inscribing scripts / delegating responsibility to artifacts can offload moral responsibility onto objects; use deliberately, aware that 'don't make me think' can wrongly strip agency.

design_principles.name: Design for multistability and what the solution can be
design_principles.gloss: Embrace ambiguity/schizofunctionality as both constraint and generative source (typewriter+TV -> PC); the design-metaphysics question is what the solution CAN be.

design_principles.name: Design the intangible systems of meaning via the thing's gathering
design_principles.gloss: Experience design works on the effects objects have on intangible systems and on how the thing 'things', attending to material AND immaterial (the jug's void).

design_principles.name: Anticipate creative misuse
design_principles.gloss: Released solutions take on new meanings; misuse reveals un-discovered needs, wants, and desires; design with this in view.

mediation_relations.name: Embodiment relations
mediation_relations.gloss: The object is fully embodied into the experience and fades out of focus; something else is experienced THROUGH the object (kin to ready-to-hand). Example: eyeglasses looked through to see the world; touch screen acted through to reach the task — until scratched/dirty. Structure: human-(technology-world).

mediation_relations.name: Hermeneutic relations
mediation_relations.gloss: The user acts WITH (not through) the object; the object becomes a focal point and must be read and interpreted to be experienced; it 'calls for our attention'. Examples: thermometer (Verbeek), Twitter — read like a text to understand the world. Verbeek: embodied and hermeneutic are 'extreme ends of a continuum'.

mediation_relations.name: Background relations
mediation_relations.gloss: Characterized by lack of conscious awareness; technologies shape the content of experience without being consciously experienced and create the context in which embodied/hermeneutic relations play out. Example: refrigerator. Wendt qualifies: difference from embodiment is proximity/direct involvement, not awareness.

mediation_relations.name: Alterity relations
mediation_relations.gloss: Technology becomes quasi-other — experienced as anthropomorphized / imbued with human-like attributes, operating on a similar yet importantly different level than the user. Example: Apple's Siri (a personality of 'her' own); 'taking care of' a car; 'intelligent machines'. 'The fantasy of much modern computing'.

ro_hooks.note: design-side analogue of the actualization-of-desire chain's refusal to treat the object as a neutral instrument; the object is a co-agent in actualizing/deflecting desire

correlate of the chain's claim that the environment/object participates in constituting (not merely presenting) the desire actualized through it; maps onto the moment a sensed object becomes a moved-toward end
maps onto the chain's inscribed-end vs actualized-end distinction; delegation fixes actualization in advance, creative misuse re-actualizes the object otherwise

design-side reading of how an environment recedes (embodied/background = unnoticed horizon for desire) or obtrudes (hermeneutic/alterity = focal object re-soliciting desire) — the engagement/boredom oscillation the dissertation tracks
